posts.name: IrisGo for Solopreneurs
posts.tagline: AI workflow automation: show it once, let it run
posts.description: IrisGo helps solopreneurs automate recurring work. Get daily briefs, triage email, track to-dos, and turn demonstrated tasks into reusable workflows with Watch & Learn. Spend less time on admin and more time building your business. Free during beta.

comments.body:
Hi Product Hunt! 👋 I’m Jeffrey, building IrisGo.

We’re launching an offering for solopreneurs and small business owners who juggle multiple roles, and spend too much time on recurring admin tasks.

https://irisgo.ai/solopreneur

If you’re spending hours each week managing your inbox, tracking priorities, summarizing meetings, preparing briefs, and filing expenses, you know it’s time that could be spent on customers and growth.


IrisGo learns these workflows by watching how you work, then automates them on your device. No repeated prompts, and your sensitive data stays on your device. Our Watch & Learn feature is central to understanding how you work, and handling that task forever. 

We’d love to learn:

  • Which of these tasks takes the most time in your day?

  • Was it clear on how to get started?

  • Where would you want more control or explanation?

Try the demo and let us know what works—or where you get stuck. We’ll be here to answer questions and learn from your feedback.


https://irisgo.ai/solopreneur

posts.name: Foley
posts.tagline: A voice to-do list that files, plans and asks first
posts.description: Say what needs doing. Foley turns it into a task with the project, date and reminder already set, and asks when it isn't sure instead of guessing. When plans change, say so and it moves the task. Ask it to plan your day, or what to work on first, and it answers from your list. Capture from your Apple Watch. The desktop app is free with no account, using your own OpenRouter key. Foley Pro runs the AI for you and syncs every device. On iPhone, Android, Mac, Windows and the web.

comments.body: Hi Product Hunt. I'm José, a software engineer with over 25 years of experience (https://www.linkedin.com/in/jose...). I kept losing tasks I said out loud: mid-meeting, in the car, walking the dog. Foley is the to-do list I wanted for that. You talk, and it files. It handles time the way people say it ("next Tuesday morning"), and it asks when it isn't sure instead of guessing. When plans change, say so and it moves the task. Ask it to plan your day, or what to work on first, and it answers from your own list. The desktop app is free with no account, using your own OpenRouter key. Foley Pro is $8 a month on the web, and your first month there is $4, applied at checkout. I'll be here all day. Tell me what it got wrong.
Using an Apple Watch to capture tasks is a nice touch. Sometimes pulling out your phone is already too much friction.
Finally an assistant can help organize the chaos in my head without making me type everything out.
can it handle task well even when plans change?

Handling relative time like "next Tuesday morning" is the part of voice capture that usually breaks first. Building voice AI for older adults, the trickiest case for us was self-corrections mid-sentence ("Thursday, no wait, Friday"). Does Foley treat the last thing said as the final intent, or does it ask you to confirm when it hears a correction like that?

"asks when it isn't sure instead of guessing" is the right default and most voice products get it backwards because asking feels like friction and guessing feels like magic, until the guess is wrong and now you've got a task filed under the wrong project with a made-up date. we fight the same tradeoff on calls at Dial. where's the line for you on what counts as "not sure", confidence score under some threshold, or ambiguity between two specific candidates like two projects with similar names?

posts.name: pmtui
posts.tagline: Autopilot for long-running AI sessions in terminal
posts.description: pmtui focuses on managing multiple agents and solving long-horizon tasks. Autopilot does what an agent loop does, except loops drift once the work runs long. So pmtui keeps the loop outside the agent and rebuilds the prompt each time from your goal and the agent's own last status. You choose how often to check back, and it only surfaces what really needs your attention

comments.body:
I manage 3-4 real projects these days, and paying constant attention to all of them is exhausting. Even with agents doing the work, I was still the one resolving every decision from Claude or Codex stopped on — including the trivial ones. That's the part I wanted to fix

pmtui runs an auto mode on top of the session. When a session stops on a decision, a 2nd claude/codex reads it, and if it's routine it answers — with the goal I set as context. You can think of it as using Claude to decide for another Claude when the decision doesn't need a human. The other half is keeping sessions alive without me. A daemon watches each tmux session and nudges it on a cadence I choose, building each prompt from that agent's own last status and my goal, instead of a generic "continue" that makes it re-plan or quit early.

posts.name: Cairo AI
posts.tagline: AI for human performance at work
posts.description: Cairo AI connects workforce analytics, skills intelligence, AI training, and simulations to help organizations develop their people. Each teammate takes a quick psychometric assessment and a weekly check-in, then gets their own trait cards, skill metrics, and AI-built development plans and practice scenarios. Spot friction, predict turnover, and test decisions like new hires before making them. Powered by Rosetta, our behavior model. Available on web, iOS, Android and Slack.

comments.body:
Hey Product Hunt! 👋 I'm Fernando Flores, founder of Cairo.

We started Cairo with a simple frustration: most companies know more about their software than about how their people actually work together. HR tools track headcount and run yearly surveys, but nobody can tell you why a great team clicks, why another one burns out, or what each person needs to grow.

So we built Cairo Teams, a Strava for human performance at work:

🧠 For every teammate: a quick psychometric assessment and a 2-minute weekly check-in unlock your own trait cards, skill metrics, and a development plan with AI-built courses and practice scenarios tailored to you.

📊 For leaders: team-level trends to spot friction early, anticipate turnover, and pressure-test decisions (like a new hire or a team reshuffle) before making them.

🔒 Privacy by design: individual check-in answers belong to the employee. Leaders only see trends, never personal responses. We think that's the only way people answer honestly.

Under the hood it runs on Rosetta, the behavior model we've been building to turn psychometric profiles into predictions about how people actually act.

Our approach evolved a lot along the way. We started closer to classic HR analytics and realized the product only works if employees want to open it, so we redesigned everything around the individual first and the dashboard second.

We've been lucky to get here with the support of the AWS Bridge Program, a research partnership with Universidad Panamericana to validate our metrics scientifically, and early customers like Swimotion who shaped the product.

It's live on web, iOS, Android and Slack.

posts.name: Hirevire
posts.tagline: Watch every applicant answer your questions
posts.description: Hirevire replaces first-round phone screens with async video, audio and text answers. Candidates need no login. New since our 2023 launch: 1. AI writes screening questions from your job title, or turns a pasted list into set-up questions. 2. AI drafts a scorecard from the job, then scores videos, answers and resumes. 3. Rerun a score with a note. General rules go to the job's scoring memory. 4. MCP server: create jobs, read scores and move candidates from Claude, ChatGPT or any MCP client.

comments.body:
Hi Product Hunt, I am Sanat, co-founder of Hirevire. We first launched here in July 2023. We are still a team of two in Mumbai: Nikhil builds the product and I do the rest.

Hirevire sends candidates a link. They record video, audio or text answers on their phone, with no login, and you review them when you have time.

The work since then has gone into making each step of setup and review take less time.

Setting up a job: type a job title and AI suggests screening questions, with a response type and duration for each one. You choose how many. If your questions are already in a Google Doc, paste the whole list and AI turns it into set-up questions, including multiple-choice options and required fields.

Setting up scoring: AI reads the job and its questions and drafts a scorecard with factors, weights and rubrics. You edit what you want. The AI then scores video and audio answers, text answers, and the candidate's resume.

Fixing a score: if you disagree with a score, rerun it and write why. If your note is a rule for the whole job, Hirevire saves it to that job's scoring memory and uses it for every future score. You can also rescore many candidates at once after you change the rubric.

Working from your AI assistant: our MCP server connects Claude, ChatGPT or any MCP client with one URL and OAuth. posts.name: Ayven
posts.tagline: Carries and drives your team's agenda
posts.description: Ayven drives your agenda. It means observing, cutting the work into pieces your team can take one at a time, putting an owner and a date on each, and filing them in Jira or YouTrack. Then it runs, tracks and talks about the work for weeks: asking whoever knows, waiting, chasing silence, moving work when someone is away. Your team answers in Slack and the board moves. Planning stops being the barrier and you ship your agenda like crazy.

comments.body:
Howard here, founder of Alknoma.

We didn't start with a product. We started with an ANNOYANCE. Agents were impressive while you were talking to them, and then, as soon as you stopped typing, they effectively disappeared.

You'd put one in Slack and end up with another bot sitting in a channel waiting for someone to tell it what to do.

You don't prompt your teammates.


So the real problem was never, "How do we make the model smarter?" It was: how do you give a language model a spine? Something that lets it chain call after call, across days and months, reaching out to different people, all without a human babysitting it.

Sounds impossible if you know from experience just how complex chaining LLM calls can be. Three things turned out to matter, and we learned each one the painful way.


1. What a piece of work actually is.

Small enough that it can be validated, iterated, executed and closed 99.9% of the time.

Too big and the agent starts hallucinating. Too small and it loses all semantic meaning.


2. Resolving time should be first-class.

A lot of work in a team is essentially waiting.

Waiting isn't failure. It's the norm. And that happens to be one of the things LLM agents are worst at. Ayven reasons about when it should wake up next, EVERY SINGLE TIME, across thousands of runs a week.

It is about recognising a deadline, annual leave, or when a teammate has gone quiet. The async gap is hard to nail down. Ayven does that.


3. What is the base unit of a fact.

In a team, things change constantly. Someone changes their mind, a deadline moves, a customer replies, a meeting gets cancelled. An agent would treat information that was true two days ago as gospel. Change is the critical signal, and that was difficult to implement when teamwork is so unpredictable. Ayven makes sure the right things change with it.


The magic moment that wowed us, and made us decide to launch Ayven: we gave Ayven the agenda for September. Nothing else. The next thing we knew, the board was full, and accurate to our plans. It put together the pieces of what execution would look like.

Later, I asked: "What's stopping us from launching on Product Hunt?" Ayven then told me about every dependencies that I did not previously know. Nobody wrote that answer. It was just the work being captured in its truest, current state.

There is a lot more to Ayven that we haven't covered here.

Talk to us if you want this deployed in your own environment. Tell us what you want it connected to.

Ask me anything :)

posts.name: Words for the Wind
posts.tagline: A virtual wind phone
posts.description: Words for the Wind is a free, private virtual wind phone. Write what you never got to say to someone you've lost, press release, and watch your words blur away on the wind. Nothing is saved or sent. No accounts, no tracking, just a quiet place to speak.

comments.body:
Hi Product Hunt 👋

In 2010, a garden designer named Itaru Sasaki put a disconnected telephone inside a white phone booth in his garden in Ōtsuchi, Japan, so he could talk to his cousin who had died. After the 2011 earthquake and tsunami, people who had lost family began traveling there to "call" the people they could no longer reach. The idea was simple: the wind carries your words to them.

Most of us can't travel to Japan, and grief doesn't wait for a plane ticket. Many of us carry words we never got to say: a goodbye, an apology, a thank you, a letter we never sent. Online tools for grief are often public, social, or built to answer back. I wanted the opposite: a place that listens and doesn't reply, and keeps nothing.

Why I built it: I was inspired by the wind phone concept (a disconnected telephone) where people can "talk" freely to anyone they miss. This is the same concept in digital form.

How it works:

  1. Write to someone you miss.

  2. Press release, and your words blur and fade away.

  3. The page forgets. Nothing you write is saved or sent anywhere.

Details I cared about:

  • A calm meadow and soft, generated music (it starts quietly, and one tap turns it off)

  • Built for accessibility: keyboard and screen reader friendly, reduced-motion support, and no information that depends on sound

  • Free to use, with an optional donation if it helps you

I'd love your feedback, especially on how the experience feels and what would make it gentler. Thank you for reading, and be kind to yourself today. 🍃

posts.description: Your headphones become a focus switch. Put your AirPods in and your Mac turns on your Focus mode, blocks distracting sites and starts a timer in the notch. Take them out: break time, sites come back. Also in the notch: now playing, volume and brightness, your own colors, session history and two tiny buddies that react to everything. comments.body:
Hi PH 👋

Honest intro: I vibe-coded Cue with Claude. I had free tokens and a habit of opening YouTube "for one second", so this happened.

The idea is small: your headphones are the focus switch.
- Put your AirPods in → Cue turns on your Focus mode (Do Not Disturb by default), blocks the sites you picked and starts a timer in the notch.
- Take them out → break. The sites come back and the buddies take a nap.

Other stuff that crept in: now playing, volume and brightness in the notch, your own notch colors, a session history, and two little buddies that react to pretty much everything. No notch? Cue draws a small floating pill instead.

Limits, so nobody is surprised:
- Apple Silicon, macOS 14+.
- Wear detection needs AirPods Pro, AirPods 3/4 or AirPods Max. Other headphones work on connect/disconnect instead.
- It is not notarized (that needs a paid developer account), so macOS asks you to click "Open Anyway" once. The site shows the steps.
- Free, closed source, made by one person plus an AI. Bugs are possible, feedback is very welcome.

Privacy: no accounts, no analytics. Cue only goes online for the feedback button and two one-time anonymous setup pings ("opened", "ready") so I know if anyone got it working. Nothing else leaves your Mac.

Would love to hear what breaks 🙏

Using the AirPods as the trigger instead of yet another toggle is such an obvious-in-hindsight idea that I'm mildly annoyed I didn't have it first 😄 The fact that taking them out *is* the break — instead of you having to remember to end a session — means the app never becomes one more thing to manage. Also appreciate you listing the limits up front (Apple Silicon, not notarized, etc.); that kind of honesty makes me way more likely to actually try something.

Blocking sites and starting the timer automatically removes the friction of setting it up each time. The little buddies in the notch are a fun touch. I would recommend to upload also EN demo video for EN version of the website. There is a higher chance to cover bigger market :)
Love the idea of making focus time this simple. No need to keep turning things on and off manually.

comments.body:
Hi Product Hunt 👋

I'm Dudley, and I'm the developer of Chunk.

Some of you might remember Chunk from the v3 launch, when it was a panel that dropped down from the menu bar. People liked the idea but kept telling me the same thing: it was great for seeing the week but restrictive for planning it. So I spent the last few months turning it into a full feature app that has the best of both worlds. 

How it works: your tasks sit on one side, your calendar on the other. Drag a task onto a time and it becomes a block. While you're in a block, a countdown tells you how long is left, and a small floating timer stays on screen even if Chunk is closed. When the block ends you get a fullscreen alert where you can tick it off, take more time or push it to later.

What's new since last time:
• A full window with three layouts: Tasks, Plan and Calendar
• Faster Apple Reminders sync, now with notes and priority
• Search across tasks, reminders and calendar events
• Priorities, links and Markdown notes on tasks
• Private iCloud sync between your Macs, no account needed
• Claude can now create tasks and move things around in your calendar for you

It syncs both ways with Google, Outlook and Apple Calendar, so it works alongside whatever you already use.

It's a one-time $29.99, no subscription, and there's a 7 day free trial with no card needed.

I'd really like to hear how you plan your days and what's missing for you. I'll be here all day answering comments.
